south_margin_finding.conclusion: South has the HIGHEST per-order margin of any region -- its revenue decline is a volume/demand problem, not a pricing/margin problem.

external_benchmark.south_growth_vs_market: far below market (-24.7% vs ~11-13%) -- company-specific, not market contraction
external_benchmark.west_growth_vs_market: below market (-1.26% vs ~11-13%) -- flattened, not growing with the category

scenario_evidence.interpretation: Fixing retention is worth more than fixing discounting, and both are worth more than spending more on marketing -- reinforcing that this is a retention/execution problem, not a demand-generation problem.

causal_chain.finding: Company revenue growth is decelerating, not reversing.
causal_chain.evidence: +98% YoY (2023->2024) slowing to +13% YoY (2024->2025); statistically confirmed deceleration, not just early-stage base effects (quadratic trend p=6.7e-11).

causal_chain.finding: The deceleration is a regional mix problem, not a market-wide one.
causal_chain.evidence: North (+31.3%) and Central (+21.6%) are growing well above the ~11-13% Indian e-commerce/retail benchmark; South (-24.7%) and West (-1.3%) are badly underperforming that same benchmark. Since the market itself grew at a normal rate, South/West's declines are company-specific execution issues, not a shrinking category.

causal_chain.finding: South's problem is volume/demand, not pricing -- it has the best per-order margin in the company.
causal_chain.evidence: South's per-order margin (32.68%) is the HIGHEST of any region (North lowest at 32.03%), though the regional spread is small (~0.6-0.7pp). Combined with churn modeling where region_South is the single strongest positive churn predictor, South looks like a traffic/retention execution gap, not a pricing problem that discounting more could fix.

causal_chain.finding: Underneath the regional story, repeat-purchase behavior is weakening company-wide.
causal_chain.evidence: Monthly customer retention fell from 13.96% to 11.98% over the tracked period, a statistically real decline (p=9.5e-12, R²=0.76), not noise. The churn model independently found 81.3% of the training cohort made no repeat purchase within 90 days.

causal_chain.finding: Margin compression compounds the revenue slowdown: heavier discounting has materially eroded profitability.
causal_chain.evidence: Gross margin fell from 34.29% (2023) to 29.47% (2025) as discount rate rose from 7.04% to 13.44% of order value. This is a real, material effect, not a coincidence: high-discount orders average 28.9% margin vs 35.61% for low-discount orders (p < 1e-300).

causal_chain.finding: Returns are rising too, adding a second (smaller) drag on margin.
causal_chain.evidence: Return rate rose from 5.22% to 7.18% of order value over the same period. Note: return_rate alone is a weak/confounded signal of customer value (Phase 08 correlation test sign-flipped between Pearson and Spearman), so this is best read as a margin drag, not an independent churn predictor.

causal_chain.finding: The financial exposure is concentrated: a specific customer segment holds most of the value at risk.
causal_chain.evidence: 8,674 customers classified High Value + High Risk hold Rs 335,678,885 (41.8% of all customer value) -- under a third of the customer base carries the largest single share of value that retention efforts could protect.

causal_chain.finding: Net result: profitability has compressed to single-digit-adjacent net margin.
causal_chain.evidence: FY2025 net margin stands at 11.06% (net profit Rs 40,691,374 on gross margin 29.47%) -- the combined effect of steps 1-7.

causal_chain.finding: Scenario testing independently confirms retention, not marketing spend, is the highest-leverage fix.
causal_chain.evidence: Modeled incremental annual profit: Retention +5pp = Rs 13,680,404; Discount -2pp = Rs 8,501,040; Marketing +25% = Rs -595,803 (essentially break-even, consistent with Phase 08's finding that marketing spend does not statistically predict performance at this sample size).
